specs.scene: A plumber's van floor doubling as a workbench, crowded edge to edge with the real gear of the trade: a pipe wrench, a coil of copper tubing, a roped bundle of Teflon tape, a battbattery drill, and a stack of blank job tickets, all overlapping with small bare patches of stained plywood showing between them. One hand reaches into frame gripping the wrench mid-turn while the other hand holds a smartphone flat against the surface, its screen turned face-down and unreadable. Hard work-light from one side, no branding or readable marks anywhere on the tools or paper.
specs.source_quote: The tool removed the build cost, it did not hand you customers

recognisable.why: Pipe wrench, copper tubing and work gloves read instantly as 'tradesperson' without any label, the familiar-trade tier the rubric rewards.

legibility.why: The props overlap into one crowded gestalt rather than several separate marks to decode, though the sheer object count keeps it just short of a single clean mass at 120px.

curiosity.why: The overlay states a flat, unresolved verdict — tools solve building, not customers — that a viewer running their own trade business would want explained.

subject.why: Hands provide a human anchor but the frame has no single dominant object, which is the flatlay's structural tradeoff against this dimension.

credible.why: No figure is carried on this frame, which the rubric scores as full since no top-quartile comp in this register carries one either.

stakes.why: Implies a real financial risk to a viewer who ships software expecting it to sell itself, without naming a number.

reexpress.why: None of the three titles mention distribution or customer acquisition, so the frame carries a consequence the title never states.
